import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 479

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/479](https://www.erdosproblems.com/479)
-/

namespace Erdos479

/--
Is it true that, for every integer $k\neq 1$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that
$2^n\equiv k\pmod{n}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_479 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (k : ℤ) (k ≠ 1),
    { n : ℕ | (2 : ℤ) ^ n ≡ k [ZMOD (n : ℤ)] }.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos479

reformulations.difference: The extended binder `∀ᵉ (k : ℤ) (k ≠ 1)` introduces a second, shadowing `k`, so the elaborated statement has an unused outer integer quantifier. The solution set also ranges over all naturals rather than explicitly positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The elaborated quantifiers are `∀ (k₀ : ℤ) (k : ℤ), k ≠ 1 → ...`, with no occurrence of k₀ in the body. Since ℤ is inhabited, this is equivalent to the source's single quantifier: specialize k₀ to 0 in one direction and ignore it in the other. Moreover, at n = 0, Int.ModEq reduces to equality, so the congruence forces k = 1, which is excluded. Thus using ℕ adds no zero solution for any permitted k. Excluding n = 1 would likewise leave infinitude unchanged. These equivalences were proved in the scratch file, including equivalence of the complete right-hand side with infinitely many solutions restricted to n > 1.
